 The 2027 Social Security ‘Trump Bump’ Adds $75 a Month - But There’s a Catch
 Paige Cerulli 2026년 11월 6일 금 오전 10:35 UTC 0 
Retirees receiving Social Security senior benefits 
should see an increase in their benefits in 2027, but according to advocates,
the increase isn't enough to help retirees cover their expenses. On October 14,
the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a cost-of-living adjustment
(COLA) increase of 3.6% for 2027. That's the largest COLA since 2023, and it
increases benefits in response to climbing inflation.
But according to advocates, the COLA falls short, and Social Security benefits
continue to lose buying power. Here's what to know about the COLA and why it may
not be keeping up with how inflation affects retirees.

 The 2027 COLA and how it affects benefits
The 3.6% 2027 COLA amounts to an average increase of about $75 per month for
retired workers, bringing average monthly benefits up from $2,095 in 2026 to
$2,170 in 2027. Since the COLA is a percentage, higher earners who receive
larger benefit checks also receive a larger COLA increase than people who
receive smaller benefit checks.
About 72 million Social Security recipients should see that increase beginning
in January 2027, while 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income
(SSI) should see the increase on December 31, 2026.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million
Americans, giving them greater financial stability," said Commissioner Frank J.
Bisignano.
The increase has been referred to as a "Trump bump," a commentator's label
reflecting the fact that the increase traces back to third-quarter Consumer
Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) data, which is
partially driven by climbing energy prices.

 What a higher COLA actually means
An increase in benefits might seem like a positive change at first glance, but
it doesn't mean that benefits actually gained ground. Since the COLA is
calculated based on third-quarter inflation, a higher COLA means that prices
rose during the third quarter.
Additionally, the COLA calculation doesn't reflect inflation changes that
occurred in the other quarters of the year. Since the COLA is only calculated
once a year and goes into effect each January, retirees may have to stretch
their budgets to pay for higher prices. For example, Social Security recipients
received a 2.8% COLA for 2026, but the war with Iran has caused gas and diesel
prices to soar this year. That's a long time for retirees to try to stretch
their budgets until the 2027 COLA goes into effect.

 Social Security's lost buying power
The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group, estimates that over the past
decade, Social Security benefits have lost 13.7% of their buying power as the
benefits haven't kept up with inflation. According to that estimate, a dollar of
benefits in 2016 is worth just $0.86 today.
To restore benefits' buying power for the average beneficiary, benefits would
have to increase by nearly $296 per month, or about $3,550 per year.
Retirees are feeling the effects of that lost buying power. A September 2026
AARP poll found that about 75% of those age 50 or older didn't feel that a 3.5%
COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
 Save Money: Things to cut when living on retirement (many people ignore #11) 
 The problem with using the CPI-W
Some advocates explain that the CPI-W is problematic, too. The National Active
and Retired Federal Employees Association (NARFE) supports the use of the
Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) in its place. The CPI-W reflects
costs paid by younger workers and, according to the NARFE, doesn't account for
seniors' spending habits, especially for their spending on health care. The
NARFE reports that seniors spend nearly double the average spending of the
general population on health care, and health care costs have also risen faster
than the cost of other goods.
The CPI-E may more accurately reflect seniors' spending costs, potentially
leading to a more accurate and larger COLA. Groups like the NARFE advocate for
its use in place of the CPI-W.
 The Medicare Part B premium effect
Medicare Part B premiums, which are deducted from Social Security benefits, may
also eat up part of the 2027 benefit increase. The official premium amounts
should be released in the coming weeks. According to the Medicare Trustees, the
monthly 2027 premium is projected to rise to $209.50, an increase of $6.60 per
month.
If the COLA already comes up short in comparison to the prices that retirees are
really paying, the fact that Medicare Part B premiums also eat into those
benefits could strain budgets even more.
 Bottom line
You may log into your my Social Security account beginning in late November to
view your COLA notice and see the exact dollar amount of your 2027 benefits. To
see the notice online, you'll need to enroll in paperless billing. If you don't
enroll in paperless billing, you'll receive your notice in the mail in December.
Once you know your benefit amount for 2027, it may be a good idea to revisit
your budget and retirement
plan to make any necessary adjustments.
